newsitem.title: HUNGARY: POOR ROADS HURT HUNGARY MINING TOWN'S REVIVAL PLAN.
newsitem.headline: POOR ROADS HURT HUNGARY MINING TOWN'S REVIVAL PLAN.

text.p: The south Hungarian town of Pecs has set up a plan to revive the region, but it also needs more political clout to convince the government to build much needed roads, officials said on Tuesday.

"Inadequate road capacity is our main drawback," Tamas Sikfoi, secretary of Pecs and Baranya County's Chamber of Industry and Commerce (PBKIK), told Reuters during a conference on investment opportunities.
"The Budapest industrial lobby has little consideration for the provinces," he said.
Pecs, once second in economic strength only to Budapest, fell back to ninth place after the nearby Mecsek coal and uranium mines were closed making some 10,000 people in the area redundant, he said.

After demolishing the disused mine buildings, there are plans to create the town's first industrial park. The cleaning up itself would create much-needed jobs, said Csaba Szirmai, vice-president of the non-profit group Work for Pecs-Baranya.

"Demolishing shaft towers or six-to-seven storey mine buildings requires special skills possessed by the miners made redundant," he said, adding that "we could offer employment for several hundred people for at least three years."

Szirmai he has applied for a 110-million-forint grant from the government job creation agency the Public Labour Council. Such aid would help rebuild the local economy and amount to more than just another handout.
"What we are offering is fishing nets, not fish, as the government does elsewhere," he said.
One foreign investor already present in Pecs said despite poor roads the town and the region has a number of advantages.

"The benefits are that you have all services available locally -- a well-developed banking system, taxes, computer support. It's all there," said Dieter Eppler, managing director of Hauni Sopiana, the Hungarian unit of Germany's Korber Group.

"Furthermore, you have a region with the highest percentage of foreign language speakers (in Hungary)," he said, adding that Pecs's Janos Pannonius University provides a steady flow of well-educated potential middle and upper level management.
But he echoed Sikfoi's concern about the region's roads, especially the main hoghway to Budapest, which for the most part is only two-lane.
"There is a lot of room for improvement," he said. "When going to Budapest (some 200 kilometers) I use the train whenever possible."
However Sikfoi said other investors, however, are also considering setting up in the region,
"One U.S.-based company has already committed itself to building a medical equipment plant, and as far as we know negotiations are in an advanced stage with an Israeli and a French company," he said.

Beside plans for the industrial park, the entrepreneurs of Pecs, which is very close to the Croatian border, hope to become involved in rebuilding the former Yugoslavia, especially Bosnia, buildong on existing trade links, nainly in food.
"We have extensive personal contacts there," said PBKIK vice-president Janos Kerenyi. "We were there even during the war and people appreciate that."
